Headline accuracy changes only modestly across pooling strategies, spanning 0.6495 to 0.7034. The highest stored accuracy comes from mean pooling without special tokens, followed by CLS pooling; max pooling and last-4-layer mean tie slightly lower, while standard mean pooling is worst on raw accuracy. However, the class-wise evidence shows that accuracy alone is misleading here. MRPC validation is paraphrase-heavy in these summaries (279 paraphrases vs 129 non-paraphrases), and three strategies—max pooling, last-4 mean, and nearly CLS/no-special mean—show extremely low non-paraphrase recall while maintaining perfect paraphrase recall. In practice, these behave like an almost-always-paraphrase classifier, so their higher accuracy is largely driven by class imbalance rather than true discrimination. Standard mean pooling reverses that pattern: it lowers headline accuracy and positive-class F1, but it is the only method with strong non-paraphrase recall and the best balanced recall across the two classes. Interpreted scientifically, pooling strategy affects MRPC performance mostly by shifting the precision-recall tradeoff and susceptibility to majority-class collapse, not by producing a large absolute gain in accuracy. Excluding special tokens gives the best top-line accuracy in the stored runs, but standard mean pooling appears less degenerate if the goal is to distinguish both paraphrases and non-paraphrases. A limitation is that the repository naming suggests similar but not perfectly identical thresholding procedures (one run explicitly uses a median threshold), so small differences may reflect both pooling and decision-threshold choices."}
